claims.text: Systematic control of annealing temperature and cooling rate governs phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA is homogenized or as-cast and contains a mixture of phases.
In situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction can monitor phase evolution during controlled thermal cycling.
The proposed experiments use repeated thermal cycles spanning multiple annealing temperatures and cooling rates under a controlled atmosphere.
Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs can contain ordered B2 and disordered BCC or FCC phases.
The relative amounts of ordered and disordered phases are sensitive to the thermal schedule.
Controlled thermal energy input changes the kinetics and thermodynamics of phase nucleation and growth.
Adjusting the thermal profile can drive the alloy toward metastable or equilibrium phases.
In situ XRD provides time-resolved structural feedback during phase transformations.
Systematically treated samples will exhibit predictable changes in phase fractions and microstructure.
Higher annealing temperatures followed by rapid cooling may stabilize metastable phases.
Lower annealing temperatures or slower cooling may promote equilibrium phases.
Conventional thermal processing without systematic control generally produces less predictable phase distributions.
The phase-control response may be sensitive to small compositional variations within the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni system.
The proposed thermal-control behavior may not transfer directly to HEAs with different elemental compositions.
The quantitative effects of particular annealing temperatures and cooling rates remain experimentally undetermined.
XRD, SEM, TEM, and hardness testing can be used to characterize phases, microstructure, and mechanical response.
Failure to obtain statistically significant or reproducible phase-evolution differences relative to conventionally processed controls would falsify the hypothesis.
